A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sparse-matrix diffusion-sampling research. Their text, equations, algorithms, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching proofs across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical constructions, results and proofs, including Appendices A–K, but no original experimental or simulation outcomes.

after.justification: v2 Section 6 and Figure 1 report original numerical experiments comparing three denoisers and examining samples generated using a trained GNN.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the Euler diffusion sampler are retained. However, Section 6 introduces a learned GNN denoiser with power-method initialization and message-passing layers, plus a spectral variant replacing eigenvector computation with 25 power iterations. These are substantive new model and inference procedures.

E1.justification: v1 studies sparse-matrix distributions analytically without empirical evaluation. v2 adds actual training and evaluation on a synthetic mixture of zero and sparse rank-one matrices, testing Gaussian denoising and diffusion generation at n = 350, k = 20.

E2.justification: v1 has no empirical comparator set. Figure 1 in v2 compares the learned GNN against the spectral-plus-projection denoiser of Algorithm 1 and its 25-step power-iteration variant. Both participate in the reported MSE comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces an empirical protocol with 10,000 training samples, 15,000 test samples, MSE evaluated across diffusion times, and generated-sample norm measurements. Training uses a 0.95/0.05 allocation above/below a changing time threshold and staged expansion from seven to ten layers. These are settings for new experiments, not revisions to experiments in v1.

E4.justification: Section 6 adds a focused diagnosis of sampling collapse through generated-sample norms. It also reports qualitative training-sensitivity observations: power-method initialization is crucial, and staged depth improves training stability. These limited analyses are not accompanied by systematic quantitative ablations or broader robustness tests.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Figure 1's histogram describes generated-sample variability, rather than uncertainty in an estimated result; theoretical concentration bounds belong under T1.

E6.justification: v2 adds the paper's first numerical results. Figure 1 reports better GNN denoising than the spectral comparators through the transition region, while all remain near MSE 0.5 below t = n/2. Generated GNN samples have norms near 0.01, and Section 6 reports a Wasserstein-distance lower bound of 0.48 versus the asymptotic prediction 0.50. These are new findings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 adds a centered-mixture definition, Theorem 6 with optimality, Lipschitz and indistinguishability assumptions, and its Appendix Q proof and auxiliary lemma. It also changes v1 Lemma 6.5's bound factor from 16 to 32 in Lemma B.5 and the associated proof. Most earlier results are retained or relocated. However, new Equations (17)–(18) impose incompatible MSE requirements over overlapping time ranges as printed.

C1.justification: The central computational-bottleneck claim remains. v2 adds a third main contribution in Section 1.2: failure of all score-matching optimizers satisfying specified Lipschitz and optimality conditions for a modified target distribution. This substantially extends v1's existence of unsuccessful near-optimizers and conditional estimation-to-sampling reductions.

C2.justification: v2 revises the stated limitations to leave successful non-Lipschitz near-optimizers open while claiming exclusion under the new Lipschitz result's conditions. It interprets the GNN experiment as predicted sampling collapse despite effective denoising. It also removes Section 3.3's explicit caveat that matching hardness results are unknown.

D1.justification: For the new experiment, v2 specifies power-method initialization, message-passing depth, two-layer LeakyReLU MLPs, a complete graph with self-loops, sample counts and training curricula. These implementation details are absent from v1. Reproducibility remains incomplete: Section 6's figure identifies an uncentered mixture, whereas its training paragraph names the centered mixture; neither version supplies code-access information.

R1.justification: v1 calls its construction novel in this context. v2 explicitly credits Koehler and Vuong (2024) with suggesting the sparse spiked Wigner example and positions its contribution as rigorous formalization and qualification of that informal observation. It also adds information-computation-gap and GNN references, substantially refining the work's positioning.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction around statistical versus computational constraints, reorganizes the contribution summary, and moves notation and main-text proofs into appendices. It adopts DS terminology and author-year citations. Appendices O/P also repeat lemma-proof material already presented in Appendix G.

P2.justification: v2 adds the two-panel Figure 1, displaying MSE curves and a generated-sample norm histogram, and introduces a table of contents. The retained algorithm boxes are compacted and relocated, while the underlying single-column mathematical-paper layout remains similar.

improvement.justification: The GNN experiment adds useful evidence from a learned denoiser beyond v1's theoretical constructions, and the revised attribution clarifies novelty. However, the important claim closing the successful-drift loophole relies on Theorem 6: Equation (17) requires MSE near 1/2 where Equation (18) simultaneously requires vanishing MSE. The experiment also inconsistently identifies its target's centering. These unresolved issues prevent a reliable net assessment of the empirical and explanatory gains against the reliability of the expanded claims.
